All weights 1 give 2 edges and all weights 2 give 7; with weights 4, 2, 2, 1, 1, 1 the heavy top node gets 4 links. Degrees match the weights only on average, so individual nodes can land above or below their pill." width="100%"} Each edge `(i, j)` is included independently with probability `w_i * w_j / sum(w)`, where `w` is the weight vector. This produces a graph whose expected degree sequence matches the given weights. Unlike `configuration_model()`, which hits a degree sequence exactly but may create self-loops and multi-edges, the Chung-Lu model matches degrees only on average and always produces a simple graph: each pair of distinct nodes is considered once, and self-loops are never created. Because the edges are independent, the model is easy to reason about analytically, and it is a common choice for: - null models that reproduce a network's degree distribution approximately - generating synthetic graphs with heavy-tailed (e.g. power-law) degrees - studying how degree heterogeneity alone affects connectivity, spreading, or centrality A few details make the realized degrees fall slightly short of the weights. There is no self-loop term, and when `w_i * w_j` exceeds `sum(w)` the probability is capped at `1`, which happens for very large weights (roughly when the biggest weight approaches `sqrt(sum(w))`). The total number of edges is about `sum(w) / 2`. Every pair is checked, so the running time grows as `n^2`. This method doesn't use or modify the graph it is called on (other than recording the step); it returns an entirely new, undirected `Graph` whose nodes are labelled `"0"`, `"1"`, ... in the order of `weights=`. The result is undirected even when the graph the method is called on is directed. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [weights]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [list[float]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : List of non-negative numbers, one per node, giving each node's expected degree (entry `i` belongs to the node labelled `str(i)`). Weights don't need to be integers. A weight of `0` gives an isolated node. At least one weight must be positive; an empty list gives an empty graph. [seed]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Integer seed for the random number generator. The same `seed=` with the same `weights=` always gives the same graph. If `None` (default), the result differs on every call. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A new undirected graph with the specified expected degree sequence. The original graph is unchanged. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If any weight is negative or all weights are zero. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} Five "hub" nodes with weight `10` and forty-five ordinary nodes with weight `2` give a total weight of `140`, so about `70` edges are expected: ::: {#4f697017 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec weights = [10] * 5 + [2] * 45 graph = ec.Graph().expected_degree_graph(weights, seed=23) graph.count_nodes(), graph.count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (50, 70) ``` ::: ::: Individual degrees scatter around their weights. The five hubs (labels `"0"` to `"4"`) land near `10`, while the ordinary nodes average close to `2`: ::: {#188383fb .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} degree = { int(graph.get_label_from_id(nid)): graph.get_degree(nid) for nid in graph.get_node_ids(limit=None) } [degree[i] for i in range(5)], round(sum(degree[i] for i in range(5, 50)) / 45, 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` ([11, 14, 10, 10, 7], 1.96) ``` ::: ::: Averaging over many seeds shows the weights acting as expected degrees. The hubs come out a little below `10` because a node is never paired with itself, so its true expected degree is `w_i * (sum(w) - w_i) / sum(w)`, about `9.3` here: ::: {#d357a899 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} totals = [0] * 50 for s in range(100): g = ec.Graph().expected_degree_graph(weights, seed=s) for nid in g.get_node_ids(limit=None): totals[int(g.get_label_from_id(nid))] += g.get_degree(nid) round(sum(totals[:5]) / 500, 2), round(sum(totals[5:]) / 4500, 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` (9.38, 1.97) ``` ::: :::
